item.title: Is Blame Culture Brainwashing Your Adult Child?
item.description:
Forgiveness

Is Blame Culture Brainwashing Your Adult Child?

An influencer with two million followers just gave your child your "diagnosis."

Posted July 25, 2026

Key points
  • It takes just 60 seconds for charismatic influencers to rewrite your adult child's family history.
  • Certainty sells because it provides instant relief at the cost of nuance.
  • Ask your child for feelings about the memory not the label.

A teary-eyed father told me his son used to say, "I'm seriously still trying to figure out what went down when you raised me." He then found a self-described "trauma-coach" on TikTok. This "coach" had no license, no credentials, just a ring light, a charismatic personality, and a huge following. The son's language and tone changed overnight to, "I now see you are a narcissist and that explains everything!"

By the way, I have seen similar situations where the newfound rattling cry out is "I'm the scapegoat," or "No contact is what I need to become my best self". Yes, maybe there are some kernels of truth if these messages resonate with adult children. But the, "This is my answer to everything that pisses me off about you" mentality is way too rigid and all-encompassing and does not lend itself to calm, constructive, healing conversations.

The 60 Second Diagnosis

In my parent coaching work, I hear many versions of what I discussed above. A daughter watches "6 Signs Your Mother Is Emotionally Immature," then "wham!" as she recognizes her mother qualifies for 3 of the 6. Yet, the other three signs completely describe someone else's mother. A son hears "3 Signs You Were The Golden Child" and "How You Were The Family Scapegoat" back-to-back and picks whichever better explains his life's struggles.

These are not clinicians building a careful case out of months (I'll settle for even some weeks) of counseling sessions. They are content creators who have learned that signed, sealed, and delivered diagnoses, offered in sixty-second reels, get clicked and virally shared. And, sadly, that leaves no room for nuance and thoughtful reflection.

Certainty Sells, Nuance Doesn't

What leaves me most concerned is that the illusion of certainty turns into accuracy when influencers provide "immediate clarity" to a long history of emotional pain and struggle. A real diagnosis takes time, effort, and someone who can really understand your family. A viral one takes a flashy hook, and the comment section is filled with "Yeah, OMG, wow, this literally describes my mom."

If this is repeated a number of times, it becomes crystallized, providing the illusion of emotional relief because "Now I finally have the answer to why my life sucks." That's closer to brainwashing than most of us want to admit. Not because anyone is lying on purpose, but because the mechanism of communication is virality, not accuracy and context.

The Pain Behind The Bind

This is why I recently wrote my book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me. It's to help parents navigate tensions and emotional reactivity from their struggling adult children. This is not about bad adult children or bad parents. It's not about "winning" by deciding who is at fault. Rather, it is about staying healthy and close in your relationship with your adult child when you are being cast as the villain.

I'm not saying to dismiss the things your adult child brings to you, though. Some of it may be accurate and overdue, and any hard truths need to be heard without defensiveness. But when the allegations come from a stranger's video rather than your actual relationship, the most useful question isn't "Is this true?" Rather, the valuable question is, "How does it fit us specifically and how can we give each other the gift of deeper mutual understanding in a respectful way that helps both of us?"

article continues after advertisement

Ask For Feelings About The Memory, Not The Label

"Please help me understand more about a specific time you felt that way" will probably get you a lot further than accepting or defending against a diagnostic term that you didn't choose. Your adult child's pain is real. The label a stranger gave them may not be. Both can be true at the same time. Where the rubber meets the road is choosing to tell them apart so the relationship can be repaired.

item.title: Why Loving a Narcissist is Like Eating a Piece of Cake
item.description:
Narcissism

Why Loving a Narcissist is Like Eating a Piece of Cake

A relationship with a narcissist will eventually leave you feeling empty.

Posted July 25, 2026

Key points
  • Narcissists may be initially charming as relationship partners but, over time will leave you hungry or worse.
  • A new study documents relationship trajectories over time based on narcissistic admiration and rivalry.
  • By knowing how to detect the turn from admiration to rivalry, you can move to more wholesome relationships.

People high in the grandiose, or self-aggrandizing, form of narcissism can charm anyone into loving them. Over time, though, that appeal is doomed to fade. The initial rush followed by inevitable disappointment is captured in what’s called the “chocolate cake model” of narcissism (Brunell & Campbell, 2011). Like eating a piece of a decadent dessert, you may be satisfied at first, but if you make this a steady diet, you'll feel just as hungry, or worse.

Narcissistic Admiration and Rivalry Spell Relationship Doom

According to new research by Michigan State University’s Gwendolyn Seidman and William Chopik (2026), the chocolate cake model is useful for understanding the inevitable reversal from desire (“spark”) to dissatisfaction (“strain”) in a relationship with a narcissist. Underlying this idea is, they believe, the even more fundamental nature of narcissistic admiration and rivalry. The Narcissistic Admiration and Rivalry Concept (NARC), as it’s called, describes the way that narcissists maintain their grandiose self-perceptions. The need for admiration leads them, at first, to be charming and engaging. Next comes rivalry, in which they turn to devaluing others and demonstrating their superiority

Translating NARC into the trajectory of a relationship with a narcissist, Seidman and Chopik note that when admiration turns to rivalry, the early attraction flips to dislike. Unfortunately, once you’re hooked to the narcissist, you may not be able to extricate yourself. In long-term relationships, narcissists become manipulative, aggressive, and less like to concede to their partners’ wishes. At the same time, they become less committed to the partner who, by now, is hooked.

Although all romantic relationships eventually settle down from their initial highs, the Michigan State authors propose that when a narcissist is involved, the downward spin will be both sharper and earlier. The “charisma” of the narcissistic partner leads to infatuation that will fade “as some of the more problematic aspects of narcissism rear their head” (p. 3).

Testing the Chocolate Cake Model Of Relationships

Using a nationally representative sample of separate birth cohorts of over 12,000 German adults studied over 14 years, Seidman and Chopik had at their disposal ample statistical power to document the downward trajectory of life with a narcissist over a period of 6 years. One person served as the “anchor” in each pairing. This led to an eventual participant pool of 5869 dyads, with a subset of people involved in new relationships of less than a year.

The analysis took advantage of the elegant APIM approach, in which both the anchors and the partners were studied in relationship to each other over time. In this case, changes in one’s own (actor) and one’s partner satisfaction could be traced in relationship to changes in the narcissistic admiration and rivalry among both members of the couple.

article continues after advertisement

The findings generally supported the NARC framework but with several twists. Rivalry scores were associated with lower relationship satisfaction, but these effects were stronger for the anchor than the partner. As the authors concluded, “narcissistic rivalry shapes how people construct their relationship experiences”… leading the highly narcissistic to expect “especially good outcomes” (p. 8).

Narcissistic rivalry, furthermore, did not moderate the drop in relationship satisfaction, as the chocolate cake model would predict. However, because the surveys were conducted at yearly intervals, it’s possible that the authors missed some key turning points in which major conflicts or transitions occurred that exposed the damaging effects of narcissism. Another possibility is that the deeply unsatisfied would no longer remain couples for the duration of the study.

Nevertheless, narcissistic rivalry maintained its position as a predictor of long-term relationship dissatisfaction. Whether the declines occurred in continuous or stepwise fashion (as during a major transition), the fact remains that a narcissistic partner is a bad bet.

The Path to Healthier Relationships

Although the Seidman and Chopik findings did not quite support the pathway from initial attraction to inevitable downfall, the idea that a partner high in narcissistic rivalry will eventually harm you was supported. In the first place, a narcissistic partner will have high expectations that, if not met, can lead to an overall pattern of devaluation. The partner could, as the authors go on to suggest, erode your sense of self-worth and autonomy. Having been hooked on this person in the early days of courting, you’ll find it difficult to extricate yourself and worse, come to believe this person’s constant fault-finding.

As you contemplate a new relationship, the findings provide you with some words of caution. That charming and engaging individual may be too good to be true. Look for signs suggesting that, even if not with you but with others, this person seeks to be the center of attention. Be on guard for when self-aggrandizement turns into devaluation of everyone else, especially you.

article continues after advertisement

What if it’s too late, and you’re in this situation now? Assuming you want to remain with your partner, try to find a way to point out the hurt it causes when your partner starts to burst your self-esteem bubble. The study’s findings suggest that there are variations in the trajectories of relationships with narcissists over time. Stepping in and trying to change that trajectory can ensure that yours doesn’t suffer the fate of the chocolate cake.

To sum up, narcissists can prove to be unsatisfying as relationship partners, but knowing the risks can help you beat the odds and find fulfillment.

item.title: Coping with Moral Distress in Healthcare
item.description:
Resilience

Coping with Moral Distress in Healthcare

How to acknowledge moral distress and build resilience.

Posted July 25, 2026

Key points
  • Moral distress--widespread among healthcare professionals--impacts well-being, retention, and patient care.
  • Morally injurious events can lead to guilt, shame, and helplessness in even the most resilient clinicians.
  • Moral injury is linked to burnout, depression, PTSD, and suicidal ideation in healthcare workers.
  • Organizational level change, Acceptance and Commitment Therapy and Trauma informed Guilt Reduction offer hope.

Sixteen years ago, I started as a psychologist at a large VA hospital. Since then, I’ve listened to hundreds of healthcare workers—nurses, physicians, social workers—describe the moments that keep them up at night. During COVID-19, I served as a consultant for the a research team in Canada to develop and test an intervention for moral distress among healthcare workers.

During the study, one nurse told our research team that, when facing moral distress, she was taught to “shove it down, suck it up, be more resilient, keep going. We are not robots. We are human beings and we have feelings and experiences.” (Smith-MacDonald et al., 2022). That line has stuck with me. It captures the reality that healthcare professionals are asked to do the impossible, sometimes at the expense of their own sense of right and wrong.

Potentially Morally Injurious Events (PMIEs)

A Potentially Morally Injurious Event (PMIE) is any situation that violates a deeply held personal value and carries high stakes (Litz et al., 2009). In healthcare, PMIEs can occur at multiple levels:

  • Individual Level: These events might involve being forced to provide care that feels futile, making decisions where all options lead to negative outcomes, or feeling powerless to act on one’s clinical judgment (Beadle et al., 2024).
  • Societal/Relational Level: PMIEs can be triggered by communication breakdowns with patients and families, responsibility for patient advocacy, or feeling unsupported by one’s own network. One healthcare worker in our Smith-MacDonald et al. (2022) study captured this: “My husband does not believe COVID-19 is real, even though I tell him I see people die every day.”
  • Organizational Level: Systemic factors like hierarchy, regulations, staffing shortages, resource constraints, and policies that prevent clinicians from acting in line with their values are frequent sources of PMIEs. As one participant in our study described, “The management does not listen. I don’t feel cared for by management” (Smith-MacDonald et al., 2022).

Moral Distress: We Hurt Where We Care

Moral distress is more than frustration or disappointment. It’s a persistent sense of guilt, shame, helplessness, disgust, or even rage. In a recent study of over 5,700 physicians, nearly 40% reported high moral distress—more than four times the rate seen in other US workers (Tutty et al., 2026).

Emergency medicine physicians and general internists were at especially high risk. The emotional toll is clear: 75% of physicians with high moral distress also reported symptoms of burnout, compared to just 31% with low moral distress. Intent to leave the profession is also higher among those with moral distress: 34.5% of physicians with high moral distress intended to leave practice within two years, compared to 18.2% with low distress (Tutty et al., 2026). This isn’t just about healthcare providers suffering—it’s about the sustainability of our healthcare system.

article continues after advertisement

Moral Injury: When Distress Becomes Disabling

Moral distress becomes moral injury when healthcare providers cope by avoiding or escaping moral pain—using survival strategies that may offer short-term relief, but ultimately increase suffering and interfere with daily functioning (Litz et al., 2009). In the intervention I co-developed with Dr. Smith-MacDonald and colleagues (2022) Several group members discussed functional impairments like burnout, anhedonia, leaving or considering leaving the profession, problematic substance use, unhealthy eating, quitting activities they used to enjoy, cynicism, numbness, isolation from family and friends, reactivity at work, and rumination and resentment towards management, fellow citizens and even intimate partners.

The consequences are serious. Moral injury is linked to higher rates of depression, PTSD, and suicidal ideation. In one study, military veterans, healthcare workers, and first responders who screened positive for moral injury had six times the odds of a suicide attempt in their lifetime and were three times more likely to have thoughts of suicide in the past two weeks (Griffin et al., 2025).

Building Resilience: What Actually Helps

Healthcare providers are resilient—after all, they have proven themselves through rigorous preparation, and have trained for hard moments. Still, individual resilience cannot compensate when the system itself is the source of the wound. Clinicians are on the front lines of American frustration with healthcare, absorbing the impact of complex systems, administrative burdens, institutional betrayal, and reimbursement structures tied to the corporatization of healthcare—all of which can create conflicts of interest (Mewborn et al., 2023). Studies show that improving ethical culture, ensuring adequate staffing and resources, transparent leadership, and closed-loop feedback systems all help reduce moral injury (D’Alessandro-Lowe et al., 2023).

article continues after advertisement

So let's support our healthcare providers by continuing to advocate for needed change in our healthcare system!
